title: Context Counts: Measuring How AI Reflects Local Realities in Education cts-local-realities-in-education.pdf
author: AI-for-Education.org
source: Fab AI / AI-for-Education.org research paper (fab-ai.org), November 21, 2025
summary: This research paper from AI-for-Education.org's benchmarks team, produced with EdTech Hub's AI Observatory, examines whether existing AI benchmarks adequately measure 'contextualisation' -- how well AI-generated educational content reflects a student's actual local environment, culture, language, and curriculum -- with a particular focus on low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The authors open with the observation that under 0.2% of AI training data comes from Africa or South America, creating a real risk that AI-generated lesson materials default to culturally alien references (their running example: a lesson plan that generates pizza instead of chapati). They define contextualisation across four dimensions -- everyday life/local environment, behaviour and identity, linguistic fit, and curricular alignment -- and then survey eight existing automated AI benchmarks (Global PIQA, EECC, BertaQA, CulturalBench, BLEnD, No Culture Left Behind, GeoMLAMA, NORMAD) to see which of these dimensions each one actually measures and where. They find substantial coverage gaps: benchmarks rarely test AI's handling of people's names, local geography, or animals, and geographic coverage of LMICs remains thin even where benchmarks exist, while behaviour/identity dimensions are comparatively better covered. Only one benchmark (EECC) targets subject-specific educational content directly, but its measurement methodology is too weak to support practical procurement decisions. The paper concludes with concrete recommendations for developers, policymakers/procurers, and the wider AI-education community, urging continued human review of AI outputs used in LMIC contexts and calling for new benchmarks that fill the identified gaps.
points: Grounding statistic driving the whole paper: less than 0.2% of AI training data comes from Africa and South America, creating a structural risk that AI-generated educational materials default to culturally irrelevant references for LMIC students.

Defines contextualisation across four measurable dimensions -- everyday life/local environment, behaviour and identity, linguistic fit, and curricular alignment -- giving procurers and developers a concrete framework rather than a vague ideal.

Survey of eight existing automated benchmarks finds systematic gaps in testing AI's use of people's names, local geography, and animals, even though these are foundational to relatable children's literacy materials.

Only one benchmark (EECC) targets subject-specific educational content directly, but its own authors acknowledge its measurement approach (lexical variance and weak correlation with cultural-values surveys) can't support a policymaker setting a minimum acceptable-use threshold.

Practical recommendation: because AI models show the steepest contextualisation drop-offs for Sub-Saharan African contexts specifically, human review of AI-generated educational outputs remains essential wherever benchmark coverage is thin -- an equity concern as much as a quality one.
quotes: [1] "While the full training data set for AI models is unknown, evidence suggests that less than 0.2% of the data (mostly text) used to train AI models comes from Africa and South America. Given this, there is a risk that the outputs from AI models will struggle to produce good examples for education in LMICs or link to the national curricula.

[2] "This challenge is broadly referred to as 'contextualisation', which we define as the extent to which an output is adapted to make it relevant to a specific audience... it has been shown that locally relevant content has been shown to affect student engagement, motivation and learning outcomes.

[3] "Whilst the majority of the benchmarks identified in Table 1 cover some aspects of every day life and the local environment, the topics are not very consistent and there are gaps in being able to measure AI ability here. Most notably, we found a gap in terms of people's names, and measuring AI's ability to use more common names in different contexts.

[4] "In their analysis, they find that AI models do adapt their outputs when prompted for different nationalities, often incorporating culturally relevant vocabulary in their responses. However, the authors found only a weak correlation between the similarity of the text outputs and the cultural values of the countries.

[5] "Whilst AI models can adapt their outputs, the existing results show significant drop offs in performance when adapting to LMIC contexts, with the worst performance often showing for Sub-Saharan African contexts. For users and policymakers, this means that additional care, and close human review, is still important when using AI to tailor outputs to a particular context.

[6] "There is no currently existing benchmark which can give sufficient confidence to users and policymakers, or that can enable developers to easily and accurately measure the quality of educational outputs adapted for all LMICs at the national level or lower.
